source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: Core statement of the theory. Jurors build a causal model of the evidence (stage 1). In parallel they learn the verdict categories from the judge's instructions (stage 2). The decision is made when the story is matched to a verdict category (stage 3). The decision rests on this intermediate summary, not on the raw evidence.
numbers: Three stages; no experimental numbers in this note.
quote: decision makers construct an intermediate summary representation of the evidence and that this representation, rather than the original "raw" evidence, is the basis of the final decision
limits: Theory statement only. Empirical numbers are in the 1986, 1988 and 1992 papers that it cites as support.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our schema: S-represent builds a story-like model, a separate step learns the answer categories, then a match step. Evidence is not decided on directly.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: The story has a fixed shape: an episode schema with initiating events, goals, actions, consequences and accompanying states in a causal configuration. Episodes nest, so a story is a hierarchy. Knowing the schema lets the juror see which parts are missing.
numbers: Episode components: initiating event, goal, action, consequence, state. Hierarchy of embedded episodes.
limits: Schema is assumed from story-grammar work, not derived from juror data in this note.
agent_relevance: A checklist of story slots (cause, goal, action, outcome, state) is a cheap completeness test the program can count, which fits G5 (code selects).

source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: Acceptance and confidence rest on certainty principles. Coverage: how much credible evidence the story explains. Coherence: completeness, consistency, plausibility. Uniqueness: whether rival coherent stories exist. If two coherent stories exist, confidence in either drops. Confidence also depends on goodness of fit to the verdict category.
numbers: Five factors listed: coverage, completeness, consistency, plausibility, uniqueness; plus fit of story to verdict.
quote: If more than one story is judged to be coherent, then each story will lack uniqueness and uncertainty will result.
limits: Principles are not formally defined here, so scoring them needs a chosen measure (see Byrne 1995 critique).
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete selection rule for S-select: score rival accounts by coverage, then penalise when a rival is also coherent. Uniqueness is a built-in reason to keep alternatives (links to Alternative-explanation controls).

source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: Stage 2 treats each verdict as a category (frame) defined by criterial features: identity, mental state, circumstances, actions, joined by and/or. Learning it is one-trial learning of abstract material. Stage 3 is a deliberate classification. If not every element is met beyond reasonable doubt, the juror defaults to not guilty.
numbers: Verdict features on four axes: identity, mental state, circumstances, actions.
limits: Default-to-not-guilty is a legal rule layered on the match, not a feature of stories.
agent_relevance: The answer-category step is separate from the story step. A default answer when required elements are unmet is a clean guard for the match operator.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: Jurors interpret abstract legal terms by placing them in the story. Example: told to judge whether the defendant had 'exhausted all means to avoid combat', jurors often decided he should never have been at the scene, and so lost self-defence. This reading is wrong in law. Atypical crimes that do not match the generic scenario (a non-ransom kidnapping) get lower conviction rates.
numbers: Qualitative; no rates given for kidnapping.
limits: Reported without sample sizes in this note.
agent_relevance: Shows a failure mode: when the category definition is abstract, the reasoner bends it to fit the story. Our match step should quote the criterion text and test each element separately.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: Authors state boundary conditions. Work is mostly on criminal trials with realistic, typical cases. Extremely violent, racially or politically charged, and emotion-provoking cases were not studied. The strategy is not claimed universal: almost every mock juror used it but a few did not do all sub-tasks. Jurors under-weight witness credibility and strength of inference chains compared with an ideal evaluator.
numbers: Sampling: representative citizens called for jury duty (size not given here).
quote: we do not claim that the decision strategy described by the Story Model is universal
limits: Self-reported limits by the theory authors.
agent_relevance: Story fit can beat evidence strength. A guard is needed so a smooth story does not outweigh weak sources (G2, G3).

source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: Pilot on judges. Four trial judges responded to two of the mock-juror stimulus trials. Judges also built narratives but reasoned backward earlier (they knew the verdict elements), spent more time on credibility and inference strength, and often matched the case to a remembered precedent ('very much like the Miller case') instead of checking elements.
numbers: 4 judges, 2 stimulus trials.
limits: Very small pilot, no systematic study.
agent_relevance: Expert version of the match step is analogy to a stored case, not feature checking against a list. Link to Case-based reasoning in this field.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: The authors position the story model against four rival families: individual differences (authoritarianism etc.), heuristic toolbox, algebraic weight-and-add models, and utility theory. They say algebraic models describe general patterns but not the comprehension and credibility processes, and could sit above the story model as a complement.
limits: Authors' own comparison; not an independent test.
agent_relevance: Story construction and weight-and-add can be used together: story for structure, counted scores for selection.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (Univ. Colorado Law Review 67)
finding: Places the story model inside a general framework, Explanation-based Decision Making (EBDM), meant for any task that needs comprehension of a complex situation (military tactics, medical diagnosis). Evidence arrives scrambled, piecemeal and gappy, and items are interdependent. The decision is made from the explanation, not the raw evidence.
numbers: Three certainty principles: coverage and coherence govern acceptance; uniqueness adds to confidence.
quote: The distinctive assumption in our explanation-based approach to decision making is the hypothesis that decision makers construct an intermediate summary
limits: Generalisation beyond juries is argued, not tested, in this essay.
agent_relevance: Direct support for using the story step as a general S-represent for messy input that arrives in an arbitrary order.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (Univ. Colorado Law Review 67)
finding: Argues against rival views using the Simpson trial. The 'meter model' (a running strength-of-belief updated by weighting and adding) and Bayesian models are said not to hold for complex legal decisions; empirical studies of mock jurors 'for the most part' do not support Bayes. A prejudice-trigger view cannot be ruled out. The authors admit the Simpson analysis is a speculative after-the-fact reading, and say prediction needs inputs about jurors and evidence they did not have.
quote: empirical studies of mock-jurors' decisions do not support this model
limits: Post hoc reading of one trial; admitted as speculative. Not a test.
agent_relevance: Warning: a story theory that is only fitted after the outcome is weak. Our scaffold should fix its scoring rule before seeing the answer (G3).

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (Univ. Colorado Law Review 67)
finding: Trial tactics follow from the model. The prosecution told one linear, time-ordered story and committed early to a detailed account of the investigation, which let the defense expose small inconsistencies between criminalists. The defense had four stories available (Simpson's own story, real killers, rush to judgment with planted evidence, bungling investigators) and avoided committing early. A story about the trial itself ('Baby Justice') is also used to frame evidence.
numbers: 4 defense stories; prosecution 1.
limits: Descriptive account of attorney behaviour.
agent_relevance: Early commitment to one detailed story gives rivals a target. Keeping several candidate accounts open and committing late supports G1 and uniqueness checks.

source: OpenLearn (Open University) Jury decision making: what's the story?
finding: Plain summary and critiques. Stage 1: infer what happened and settle on a story. Stage 2: the judge links verdicts to facts. Stage 3: apply categories to the preferred story, likened to a syllogism. Critiques: thin on group deliberation (11-1 can flip to 12-0); formalist, so extra-legal factors are hard to explain; unclear what the narrative form adds because the same model can be written in other forms.
numbers: No experimental numbers on the page.
quote: Story model theories admit that the theory is a little bit thin on this group aspect of jury decision-making.
limits: Teaching text, not a primary source; read through a fetch tool that summarised it.
agent_relevance: The critique that narrative form adds nothing beyond the content matters: the benefit for our agent may come from coverage counting, not from story form.

source: Czaban (ELTE) summary of the Hastie & Pennington order-of-evidence experiment
finding: Reports the order-of-evidence experiment. Mock jurors heard 100 statements, 50 prosecution and 50 defense, identical across conditions. Each side's statements were in story order or witness order. Conviction rates: prosecution story order with defense witness order 78%; prosecution witness order with defense story order 31%; both story order 59%; both witness order 62%. Source cited is the Hastie & Pennington 2000 chapter.
numbers: Conviction: P story/D witness 78%; P witness/D story 31%; both story 59%; both witness 62%. 50 + 50 statements. N per cell not given.
limits: Secondary (law-journal article in Hungarian, read in the original). Cell sizes and test statistics not given. Attribution to one paper is uncertain; see the next-but-one line on the blog account.
agent_relevance: Order that makes a story easy to build changes verdicts with the content fixed. Reorder input into causal-time order before judging, and test with both orders (G3 mutated input).

source: Onfiction.ca blog 'juries and stories' (via WebFetch summary)
finding: Blog summary of Pennington & Hastie 1988: a real case (Johnson killed Caldwell), 119 statements derived from the trial, presented one witness at a time. Exp. 1: after the verdict, an unexpected memory test; guilty-verdict jurors remembered more prosecution-story items and claimed more inferences from it, and not-guilty jurors showed the mirror pattern. Exp. 2: story vs witness order; 78% and 31% extremes; most confidence when evidence came in story order.
numbers: 119 statements; extremes 78% guilty vs 31% guilty.
limits: Blog, summarised by a tool, not the paper. The 119 statements differ from the 100 statements in the Czaban account; the two may describe different experiments or sources. Needs the original.
agent_relevance: Verdict-congruent memory and false inferences mean the story reshapes what is stored. Keep the raw evidence list fixed and re-check claims against it (G2).

source: Hastie & Pennington 2000 chapter as relayed by Czaban: coherence suppresses doubt; defense stories and opening statements
finding: Secondary claims drawn from the Hastie & Pennington 2000 chapter: weight of evidence is judged by how well it fits the story, not alone. When the prosecution tells one coherent story, a defense that offers a weaker rival story of its own tends to do worse (more guilty verdicts). Putting a story in the opening statement primes jurors to read later evidence through it. Coherence is not a reliable sign of truth (a conspiracy theory can be very coherent).
limits: Second-hand; original numbers not seen.
agent_relevance: Coherence is not truth. Fits G3: a pass must come from something the story was not built from.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1992) Explaining the evidence: tests of the Story Model for juror decision making (abstract via synapsesocial)
finding: Three mock-juror experiments. Exp. 1: making the story easier to build (story order) changed verdicts and the effect of credibility evidence, while memory for the evidence was equal across conditions. Exp. 2 and 3: global end-of-case judgments followed the Story Model; item-by-item judgments after each evidence block fit linear anchor-and-adjust models better. Compared with Bayesian and linear updating models.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract page (DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.62.2.189).
limits: Abstract only; full paper behind paywall and not read. The task changes the strategy: asking for a judgment after each block pushed jurors toward linear updating.
agent_relevance: Evaluating after each step may switch the reasoner to a weaker, order-sensitive strategy. Link to Bessis 2026 (intermediate rating raised final ratings in GPT-4o). Rate once at the end, from the whole story.

source: Diverging Decisions? A Comparison of Jury Verdict Procedures (Behav Sci 2025), literature review passage
finding: Review text on the story model. In Pennington & Hastie 1992, mock jurors made decisions more in line with the evidence, and with more confidence, when evidence came in chronological narrative form rather than split by legal issue; item-by-item presentation lowered confidence. Pennington & Hastie 1988: better recognition for evidence matching the verdict, and false recall of things never presented if they fit the narrative.
limits: Secondary summary; no sample sizes. Their own study is about special verdict forms, not a test of the story model.
agent_relevance: False recall of story-fitting items is a hallucination-like risk: a story fills gaps with plausible inferences that become remembered as facts. Tag inferred items as inferred.

source: Verdict spotting study (mock jurors, pre-trial bias, evidence anchors, verdict system), PMC9310652
finding: A 2022 mock-juror study read through the story model. It says the model has been the most dominant juror model for almost 30 years. Narratives rest on case information, knowledge of story structure and knowledge of similar events. Pre-trial bias can shape the story. The authors say the findings lend some support and argue a 3-verdict system (adds not proven) lets stories map to a better-fitting category than a binary system.
quote: The findings of the current study lend some support for the story model
limits: Interpretation after the fact; the study did not manipulate story variables, so it is weak evidence for the model.
agent_relevance: More verdict categories can reduce forced misfit. Offer 'cannot tell' as a real answer category, not only yes/no.

source: Byrne (1995) The convergence of explanatory coherence and the story model: a case study in juror decision
finding: First computational test of the story model. ECHO networks (explanatory coherence) were built from the causal stories that two real mock jurors from Pennington & Hastie 1993 gave verbally. Juror 109 chose not guilty by self-defence; Juror 128 chose first-degree murder; same evidence. In both cases the network's highest-activation verdict matched the juror's actual verdict. Linking each story to the 19 testimony propositions raised coherence for both, even though the testimony was inconsistent.
numbers: Juror 109: 26 propositions, 18 explanations, 7 links to verdict categories, 19 to testimony. Juror 128: 19 propositions, 14 explanations, 8 verdict links, 18 testimony links. Verdict categories added 18 propositions and 7 links; final verdicts 4 propositions and 5 contradiction links. Activations range -1 to +1.
limits: Only 2 jurors, both at the extremes (no manslaughter or second-degree jurors). Table values garbled in text extraction, so exact activations not recorded. Stories were coded from verbal reports by the author.
agent_relevance: A working formal model of selection exists: spreading activation over explain and contradict links, verdict = highest activation. This can be coded as the program's select step.

source: Byrne (1995) critique of the story model
finding: Critique in this paper. The story model is an account more than a prediction: coherence, completeness and uniqueness are not formally defined, so many readings are possible after the verdict is known. ECHO gives a computed coherence per verdict. Also: in Pennington & Hastie 1986, differences in how jurors represented the verdict categories were not associated with differences in decision outcomes. The author answers the charge of programmer bias by using juror-supplied stories.
quote: the Story Model is more an account than a predictive model
limits: Author is a proponent of the merger; two-juror sample.
agent_relevance: Define the scoring rule in code before use. Verdict-category representation mattered less than story content in this data, so spend effort on the story step.

source: Thagard (2003) Why wasn't O.J. convicted? Emotional coherence in legal inference
finding: Tests four explanations of the Simpson acquittal with code. ECHO with the evidence and the defense's competing hypotheses accepts that Simpson was the killer (and also that LAPD framed him), so explanatory coherence alone does not reproduce the jury's verdict. A Bayesian network (JavaBayes) with 60 hand-set conditional probabilities points the same way.
numbers: ECHO: guilty accepted. JavaBayes: P(OJ killed)=.72, P(drug killings)=.29, P(LAPD framed)=.99. Network needed 60 conditional probabilities.
quote: ECHO, unlike the jury, finds Simpson guilty.
limits: Inputs are the author's own coding of the case and probabilities were 'guesses at best'; one case; the reasonable-doubt standard may explain the gap.
agent_relevance: A coherence-maximising selector can pick an answer that fails a legal standard needing more than best story. Keep a separate burden-of-proof check (default answer when unmet).

source: Thagard (2003) formal model
finding: The theory of explanatory coherence has seven principles: symmetry, explanation (fewer hypotheses explaining means higher coherence), analogy, data priority, contradiction, competition (rival explainers of the same fact that are not connected are incoherent), acceptance. ECHO updates activation a_j(t+1) = a_j(t)(1-d) + net_j(max - a_j) if net_j > 0, else net_j(a_j - min), with decay d about .05, range -1 to 1. Competition is the formal form of the story model's uniqueness; data priority is the form of coverage. Presumption of innocence is modelled by suppressing guilt hypotheses.
numbers: d about .05; activations in [-1,1]; 7 principles.
limits: Formal model of coherence, not a fit to juror data in this paper.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact update rule and a clean mapping from story-model terms to code (coverage = evidence links; uniqueness = competition links).

source: Thagard (2003) emotional coherence and polls
finding: Evidence that the acquittal had an emotional and group component. Defense consultant polls: 20% of a sample thought Simpson innocent and 50% did not want to believe him guilty; only 3% of 200 African-Americans assumed guilt; 75% of Black Los Angeles county respondents in an LA Times poll believed he was framed. Thagard adds valences to ECHO (HOTCO) so liking a person biases which hypothesis is accepted. Cochran: a trial is 'a struggle between opposing stories'.
numbers: 20%, 50%, 3% of 200, 75% (poll figures reported second-hand from trial books).
quote: a trial is not really a struggle between opposing lawyers but between opposing stories
limits: Poll numbers come from books by trial participants; not peer-reviewed data.
agent_relevance: Motivated coherence is real: what the reasoner wants to be true shifts which story wins. Our agent should not carry a preferred answer into the select step (G5, G4).

source: Bessis, Wills, Wojciechowski, White, Pothos (2026) Legal Decision Biases in GPT: A Comparison with Human Judgment (Behav Sci 16:437)
finding: Not a story-model test, but the closest measured LLM study on evidence order in legal judgment. GPT-4o and GPT-5.2 rated guilt (1-10) for six simplified Polish criminal cases with incriminating (G) and exonerating (I) parts in two orders, with or without an intermediate rating. GPT-4o showed a strong recency effect: guilt higher when incriminating evidence came last.
numbers: GPT-4o baseline, mean final guilt (n, SD): G-I double 4.24 (181, 2.28); G-I single 3.54 (175, 2.44); I-G double 6.04 (184, 2.01); I-G single 4.77 (180, 2.31). Order effect F(1,711)=424.76, p<.001. Rating-condition effect F(1,711)=181.11. Order x rating F(1,711)=43.75. 720 trials per model.
limits: In the paper's labels 'I-G' means the incriminating part came last. Simplified cases, single rating scale, temperature 1; human data from a separate Polish study.
agent_relevance: Order effects of about 1.3 to 1.8 scale points in a strong model: an agent must be tested under both evidence orders and must not trust one reading (G3, G4).

source: Bessis et al. (2026) GPT-5.2, humans, prompt engineering
finding: Newer model, smaller bias. GPT-5.2 still showed an order effect but much weaker, and no uniform evaluation bias. Humans (legal professionals and non-lawyers) also showed recency. Prompt engineering (expertise framing, careful deliberation, explicit justification) barely helped: only one variant (PE2) reduced the order effect in GPT-4o.
numbers: GPT-5.2 means: G-I double 4.75 (174); G-I single 4.79 (198); I-G double 5.35 (172); I-G single 5.02 (176). Order F(1,711)=71.24; rating F(1,711)=8.43, p=.0038. Humans: G-I double 4.00; G-I single 4.54; I-G double 5.77; I-G single 5.38; order F(1,686)=54.40, p<.001; 120 participants, 715 final judgments. Order x subject F(2,2138)=17.31. PE2 reduced order effect by 0.32 (SE .11, p=.003); PE1 -0.19 (p=.075), PE3 -0.16 (p=.12). Temperature 0.2 vs 1 correlation of cell means: r=.996 (GPT-4o), .989 (GPT-5.2).
limits: Single prompt family per condition.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording is a weak fix; order sensitivity is not a temperature artefact. Supports G1 and G3 over prompt-based debiasing, and supports re-ordering the evidence by program.

source: Bessis et al. (2026) evaluation bias
finding: Asking for an intermediate guilt rating changed the final rating in GPT-4o: final guilt was higher whenever an intermediate judgment was required, in both orders. In GPT-5.2 the effect appeared only when incriminating evidence came last. In humans the intermediate judgment amplified the most recent evidence (interaction F(1,709)=8.53, p=.004). This echoes Pennington & Hastie 1992, where per-block judgments gave linear anchor-and-adjust behaviour.
numbers: GPT-4o: single vs double 3.54 vs 4.24 (G-I) and 4.77 vs 6.04 (I-G). GPT-5.2: G-I 4.79 vs 4.75 (no change); I-G 5.02 vs 5.35.
limits: Not the same measure as story-model tests; shows the process effect only.
agent_relevance: Do not ask the model for interim verdicts. Keep interim scores in code and out of the context that the final answer is made from.

source: Dalal, Valentino, Freitas, Buitelaar (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (ACL)
finding: IBE-Eval scores competing LLM-written causal explanations with code: logical consistency (Prolog proof), parsimony (proof depth, concept drift), coherence (entailment per step) and hedging language. These features select the right explanation up to 77% of the time on COPA and E-CARE, 27 points over chance and 17 over a GPT-3.5 judge. This is a coverage-and-coherence selector in the story-model sense, used on LLM text.
numbers: Accuracy up to .77 (GPT-3.5 with all features on COPA); chance .50; average +17.5 points over the GPT-3.5 judge. Two humans picked the correct explanation 96% (COPA) and 91% (E-CARE) of the time on 100 sampled pairs.
limits: Causal question answering, not trials. Table text partly garbled in extraction, so only headline numbers recorded. Logical consistency alone was weak.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G5: select by counted coherence features, not by a model judge. Parsimony and coherence beat consistency.

source: Dalal et al. (2024) over-rationalisation
finding: LLMs make a consistent story for any hypothesis. Consistency scores were about the same for correct and wrong options, so consistency alone is a weak signal. For wrong options models add more steps and concepts: proof depth about 6% and concept drift about 10% higher than for correct options. Bigger models over-rationalised more. Hedging words were more frequent for less plausible hypotheses.
numbers: Depth +6%, drift +10% for incorrect options; linguistic uncertainty was the strongest single predictor in the regression.
limits: Only GPT-3.5, LLaMA 2 7B and 13B; two benchmarks.
agent_relevance: A model can build a coherent story for the wrong answer. Coherence must be paired with coverage of fixed evidence and a count of extra assumed steps (penalise stories that need many added inferences).

source: Douven (2026) Abduction In Silico: LLMs Replicate Human Inference to the Best Explanation (Minds and Machines 36:47)
finding: Replicates Douven & Mirabile (2018) with 16 models from 7 developers. Three experiments: sensitivity to explanation quality, suppression of an explanation by an alternative, and link between quality gap and confidence. New materials were written to avoid training-data contamination. Models reproduce the human patterns on both old and new materials, and sit within the range of individual human variation.
numbers: 16 models, 7 developers, 3 experiments; temperature 0 because temperature 1 gave almost no variability.
limits: Abstract and notes only (paywalled); effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Suppression of an explanation by a rival matches the story model's uniqueness principle, and LLMs show it. An LLM can serve as story builder, but selection should still be coded.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1986) Evidence evaluation in complex decision making (JPSP 51:242)
finding: Founding paper. Known only from secondary text: used a murder case (Johnson and Caldwell) with four verdict options (first-degree, second-degree, manslaughter, not guilty). Jurors gave verbal protocols; the stories were coded as causal event chains. Differences in verdict-category representation were not linked to verdicts (per Byrne 1995).
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Paper not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Must be read in full before final use (a later pass).

source: Pennington & Hastie (1988) Explanation-based decision making: effects of memory structure on judgment (JEP:LMC 14:521)
finding: Memory study of the same paradigm. Secondary reports: after a verdict, jurors recognise more evidence that fits their own verdict story and wrongly accept story-fitting inferences.
numbers: Not read; numbers only from secondary sources.
limits: Paper not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Source for the 'story reshapes memory' claim; verify before relying on it.

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction; Simon, Snow & Read (2004) The redux of cognitive consistency theories
finding: Follow-on work (cited in the Czaban paper) holds that the conclusion also shapes how premises are judged: evidence is re-weighted toward the leading verdict during the task, a constraint-satisfaction account of coherence shifts.
numbers: Not read here; Crossref citation counts 269 and 203.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Real risk for G2 and G3: once a leading answer exists, evidence is re-read to fit it. Freeze evidence ratings before candidate answers are formed.
